stories.title: John McCullough of Kennedy Wilson Multifamily Development: 5 Questions
stories.excerpt: Since joining Kennedy Wilson following the firm’s $347 million acquisition of Toll Brothers’ apartment living platform in 2025, John McCullough has been serving as president of the real estate investment company’s multifamily development group, where he oversees every aspect of the firm’s U.S. development business. Kennedy Wilson’s acquisition of Toll Brothers’ platform gave it general partner interests in 18 apartment and student housing properties, with assets under management of $2.2 billion. The firm also purchased a pipeline of 29 development sites in various stages of construction. Toll Brothers’ entire apartment living management team has transitioned over to Kennedy Wilson under the leadership of McCullough, who previously led apartment living operations at Toll Brothers. But McCullough’s real estate path wasn’t always laid out for him, as he started out in the U.S. Navy and then eventually hit his business stride at school in Boston. Commercial Observer caught up with McCullough last month to discuss his entry into real estate, the Toll Brothers acquisition, and his mission at Kennedy Wilson. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: How’d you get started in real estate? John McCullough: I got started in real estate in a roundabout way. I went to the United States Naval Academy for my undergrad, and graduated in 1994, and then served five years in what we would refer to as the surface navy. If I had stayed in the Navy long-term, I would have trained to be the captain of a ship. I served on two large aircraft carriers out in San Diego, and it was a great experience. It was a really good grounding in the fundamentals of leadership I was put into a lot of situations that were incredibly difficult as a 23- or 24-year-old, but I learned a lot from that. Then I got out of the Navy and I went to business school at Boston University, and it was during that time that I started thinking that real estate could be a really int
bullets: Kennedy Wilson acquired Toll Brothers' apartment platform for $347M in 2025; assumes $2.2B AUM.
Pipeline includes 29 development sites across various construction stages; 18 existing apartment/student housing properties.
McCullough leads multifamily development group; entire Toll Brothers apartment team transitioned to Kennedy Wilson.
stories.summary: Kennedy Wilson completed its $347 million acquisition of Toll Brothers' apartment living platform, gaining control of 18 operational apartment and student housing properties ($2.2B AUM) and a 29-site development pipeline. John McCullough, former head of apartment operations at Toll Brothers, now leads Kennedy Wilson's multifamily development group and oversaw the team transition. The deal consolidates significant development capacity and operating assets under unified management.
stories.impact: Toll Brothers' exit from multifamily development narrows the competitive landscape for large-scale development; Kennedy Wilson's expanded pipeline and AUM signals capital availability for ground-up development and value-add repositioning across major markets. Watch for where the 29 pipeline sites are concentrated—likely signals institutional deployment priorities and potential supply inflection points in those submarkets.

stories.title: Southern Land Company Hires Tony Marchbanks as Head of Homebuilding
stories.excerpt: Southern Land Company has made a leadership hire to spearhead single-family home development in three key states, Commercial Observer has learned. Tony Marchbanks has joined the firm as national president of homebuilding, in which he will focus not only on the U.S., but also focus particularly on Tennessee, Texas and Colorado, according to Southern Land. Marchbanks brings with him 30 years of real estate experience and most recently served as chief operating officer for Highland Homes, where he launched a building spree in the Houston market, producing 1,000 homes per year, Southern Land said. “Higher interest rates and lack of job growth all culminate into a lack of consumer confidence, so you have all three key contributors to a good homebuilding environment that are headwinds at this time,” Marchbanks told CO. “But for a company like Southern Land, it’s actually a huge opportunity because they have expansion plans, particularly into Texas, which is the largest new home market in the country,” Marchbanks said. “Most builders secured their lot supply three years ago, and now they have too many lots. So it’s an opportunity for a company like Southern Land to find and [invest] in communities they wouldn’t have been able to in a strong market.” Southern Land is currently developing four master-planned communities across 5,000 individual lots in its portfolio. Marchbanks will oversee the construction, purchasing, sales and architecture for those soon-to-be neighborhoods. Southern Land has been making some changes in recent months by launching its own mortgage lending division in May to augment its sales division and support its construction pipeline, CO reported at the time. Build-to-sell homes are not the only residential asset class Southern Land has been dabbling in either, as it builds multifamily properties in Las Vegas; Erie, Colo.; and just outside Austin, Tex. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Tony Marchbanks joins Southern Land Co. as national president of homebuilding; 30 years industry experience.
Focus: Tennessee, Texas, Colorado; Marchbanks previously launched 1,000-home/year program at Highland Homes (Houston).
Insight: Most builders locked lot supply 3 years ago; current oversupply creates M&A and consolidation opportunity.
stories.summary: Southern Land Company hired Tony Marchbanks, former Highland Homes COO, as national president of homebuilding to drive expansion in Tennessee, Texas, and Colorado. Marchbanks noted that higher rates, weak job growth, and low consumer confidence create headwinds broadly, but represent opportunity for well-capitalized operators. Most competitors secured lot supplies three years ago and now carry excess inventory, creating competitive advantage for Southern Land's expansion into Texas—the nation's largest new home market.
stories.impact: Single-family builder consolidation and lot repositioning (Texas especially) signals capital efficiency and land-cost deflation in key Sun Belt markets. For multifamily: builder distress and lot oversupply may lower raw land valuations in Texas/Tennessee/Colorado, improving development margins for apartment projects competing for similar suburban and infill locations. Weak consumer confidence also dampens housing demand broadly—an indirect signal that multifamily rental demand may accelerate as affordability-conscious household formation favors leasing over ownership.

stories.title: How Trent Johnson, Brian Landrum at Harbert Management Corp. Invest in Senior Housing
stories.excerpt: Trent Johnson and Brian Landrum are senior managing directors and co-heads of the seniors housing team at Harbert Management Corporation, an $8 billion alternatives asset management firm founded in 1993. The group has been investing in the seniors housing space for 15 years, raising a $210 million investment fund in 2016 and a $510 million investment fund for the space in 2020. The group is currently on its third fundraise, as they attempt to capitalize on the first wave of Baby Boomers turning 80-years-old in 2016. The duo sat down with Commercial Observer to discuss their careers, how the asset class has evolved, the present and future of the senior housing space, and where the best investment opportunities will be in an increasingly important asset class. (This conversation has been edited for length and clarity) Commercial Observer: How long have you been involved in the senior housing space? Trent Johnson: I started investing in the space in 2012, which is where I met Brian at Fortress Investment Group. I actually came from a legal background. I started out as a real estate lawyer, and then I spent a lot of years at an apartment investment and management company, which was a large multifamily REIT based out of Denver, Colo, Apartment Investment and Management Company. I was recruited away to start and lead a seniors housing platform in Dallas, which is where I joined forces with Brian, and we co-headed that office here in Dallas. Brian Landrum: I started investing in seniors housing in 2009 at a predecessor firm, Walton Street Capital, which was a diversified real estate private equity firm, and then in 2012, I joined forces with Trent in 2012 at Fortress Investment Group, which is where we began working together, and then ultimately, made a decision to join up at Harbert Management Corporation in 2015. bullets: Harbert Management raised $510M seniors housing fund in 2020; currently on third fundraise.
15-year track record; first Baby Boomers turned 80 in 2016—demographic wave underway.
Trent Johnson, Brian Landrum co-lead $8B alternatives manager's seniors housing strategy.
stories.summary: Harbert Management Corporation, an $8 billion alternatives asset manager, has invested in seniors housing for 15 years and raised $210 million (2016) and $510 million (2020) dedicated funds. The firm is now in its third fundraise to capitalize on Baby Boomers reaching age 80, which began in 2016. Co-heads Trent Johnson (legal background, investor since 2012) and Brian Landrum (from Fortress) lead the seniors housing team.
stories.impact: Institutional capital actively fundraising for seniors housing underscores strong conviction in demographic tailwinds and ROI potential in an aging-in-place market. For multifamily developers: seniors housing and assisted living represent a parallel asset class attracting institutional LP capital; the competitive landscape for land, construction labor, and financing may tighten in secondary markets where seniors housing and traditional rental development compete for sites. Monitor Harbert's deployment for signals on which metros/submarkets offer best risk-adjusted returns.

stories.title: Sunday Summary: The Rent is Too Damn Low!
stories.excerpt: Back in 2010, Jimmy McMillan ran for governor of New York on a pretty straightforward platform: The rent was too damn high. McMillan said it again and again, and named his political party The Rent is Too Damn High Party. (McMillan’s presence on the debate stage garnered national attention and Matthew Yglesias even titled a slim book with the same name.) Sixteen years later, McMillan is still not wrong, in that the average monthly rent just hit $6,655 in Manhattan according to research from Corcoran Sunshine — which is 10 percent higher than it was a year ago. There are a number of solutions that the Mamdani administration have proffered, but one that has perhaps attracted the most attention has been freezing rents on rent-stabilized apartments. In June, the Rent Guidelines Board issued a freeze on one- and two-year leases, which will certainly be popular with rent-stabilized voters. But one has to wonder if it will actually address the larger issue of affordability — especially if landlords begin to lose more money than they make on stabilized units. Some landlords are keeping units off the market rather than getting them in rentable shape. “Some of [the rent-stabilized units] require more work than others, but for the ones that need significant work — and I mean baseline, just to get them up to livable standards — we’re talking $30,000 minimum,” said Jose Tur, who owns two stabilized buildings in Washington Heights and testified before the RGB before their vote. In addition to the baseline, Tur told Commercial Observer that he would probably have to include another $30,000 per unit for the cosmetic fixes. And that’s on the lower end of the renovation spectrum. Matthew Engel, president of Langsam Property Services, says he has units that require $80,000 to $100,000 worth of work, and rent as low as $600 per month. “There’s no way for me to finance that work,” said Engel. “No bank would lend me $100,000 if I’m only going to be able to collect $6,000 a year in rent.”
bullets: Manhattan average rent hit $6,655/month in 2026; 10% YoY increase per Corcoran Sunshine.
Rent Guidelines Board froze one- and two-year stabilized lease rents in June 2026.
Policy risk: stabilized units losing money may be withheld from market; affordability crisis ongoing.
stories.summary: Manhattan's average monthly rent reached $6,655 in 2026, up 10% year-over-year, according to Corcoran Sunshine research. The Rent Guidelines Board issued a freeze on one- and two-year rent-stabilized leases in June 2026 to address affordability concerns. However, the freeze risks pushing landlords to keep stabilized units off the market if they become cash-flow negative, potentially worsening supply constraints and affordability.
stories.impact: Rent freeze on stabilized stock signals regulatory risk and potential supply withdrawal in Manhattan; multifamily developers will face stricter rent-control regimes and reduced incentive to maintain/upgrade legacy buildings, pushing institutional capital toward new construction (exempt from stabilization) and market-rate value-add repositioning. Expect accelerated conversion of Class B stabilized buildings to mixed-income or market-rate, and heightened competition for new development sites with favorable regulatory pathways (Brooklyn, Queens submarkets). Cap rates and NOI sensitivity to rent-control policy shifts will affect refinancing availability and investor appetite.

stories.title: AI-Native Hanover Park Leases Full Floor at 387 Park Ave. South
stories.excerpt: A new lease with AI-native fund administrator Hanover Park and the expansion and extension of PMG Worldwide’s existing space have been recent highlights at TF Cornerstone’s 387 Park Ave. South, which has seen more than 100,000 square feet of leasing activity in the past year. The recent transactions follow K Health’s long-term renewal and the expansion of another TAMI user completed in late 2025. Hanover Park signed a lease for the building’s entire 10th floor, totaling approximately 19,269 square feet. PMG Worldwide renewed its lease on the entire second floor while expanding into the entire third floor, bringing its total footprint to approximately 38,744 square feet. “We’re pleased to welcome Hanover Park to 387 Park Avenue South and to expand our relationship with PMG Worldwide,” said Joe Lanzilotta, Director, Commercial Asset Management at TF Cornerstone. “The property continues to outperform the market as a destination for growing businesses.” The post AI-Native Hanover Park Leases Full Floor at 387 Park Ave. South appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: AI-native Hanover Park leased entire 10th floor (19,269 SF) at 387 Park Ave. South (TF Cornerstone).
PMG Worldwide renewed 2nd floor, expanded to 3rd floor; total footprint 38,744 SF.
Property logged 100K+ SF leasing in past year; strong demand from TAMI/tech tenants.
stories.summary: TF Cornerstone's 387 Park Avenue South in Manhattan signed Hanover Park (AI-native fund administrator) for the entire 10th floor (19,269 SF) and expanded its existing relationship with PMG Worldwide to include the entire second and third floors (38,744 SF total). The property has generated over 100,000 SF of leasing activity over the past year, with recent tenants including K Health and other TAMI (Technology, Advertising, Media, Information) users.
stories.impact: Strong office leasing velocity for TAMI/AI-native tenants signals sustained demand for Class A office space in Manhattan's Flatiron/NoMad submarket; however, office-to-multifamily conversion opportunities may emerge if office supply softens. For multifamily developers: co-tenanting patterns show concentrated AI/fintech hiring and expansion in Manhattan—ground-truth indicator of high-income household in-migration and rental demand in walkable, transit-rich neighborhoods. Monitor conversion projects in office-heavy submarkets.

stories.title: PMB, Loma Linda University Health Break Ground on Inpatient Rehab Hospital
stories.excerpt: PMB, a leading healthcare real estate developer, and Loma Linda University Health with Lifepoint Rehabilitation, a business unit of Lifepoint Health, recently broke ground on a new, 99,000-square-foot, 80-bed inpatient rehabilitation hospital in Redlands. Located at 11207 New Jersey., the three-story facility will function as a standalone hospital. “Breaking ground today represents far more than just laying the foundation for a new building – it’s a promise to the community,” said Nolan Weinberg, SVP of Development for PMB. “Inpatient rehabilitation is a critical bridge between acute medical recovery and returning to everyday life..” Loma Linda University Rehabilitation Hospital will be jointly operated by Loma Linda University Health and Lifepoint Rehabilitation. A summer 2028 opening is expected. Upon completion, Loma Linda University Health will transition its existing inpatient rehabilitation unit to the new facility. PMB’s partners on the project include general contractor Layton Construction, architect Material Design Architects and financing partner Harrison Street Asset Management. The post PMB, Loma Linda University Health Break Ground on Inpatient Rehab Hospital appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: PMB and Loma Linda University Health broke ground on 80-bed inpatient rehab hospital; Redlands, CA.
99,000 SF, three-story facility; summer 2028 opening; Lifepoint Rehabilitation operates.
Harrison Street Asset Management provides financing; Layton Construction general contractor.
stories.summary: PMB and Loma Linda University Health broke ground on a 99,000-square-foot, 80-bed inpatient rehabilitation hospital at 11207 New Jersey in Redlands, California. The three-story standalone facility is expected to open in summer 2028 and will be jointly operated by Loma Linda University Health and Lifepoint Rehabilitation. Financing is provided by Harrison Street Asset Management.
stories.impact: Healthcare real estate development in Inland Empire/Redlands signals institutional capital and healthcare operators entering secondary Sun Belt markets with aging demographic tailwinds. For multifamily developers: hospital and senior housing campuses generate ancillary demand (medical professionals, patient families, nearby service workers); ground-truth indicator of population growth and household formation in Redlands submarket. Monitor hospital workforce and supplier logistics for labor availability and construction cost inflation in the region.

stories.title: Astoria Favorite :3Coffee Roasters Expands to Halletts Point
stories.excerpt: The Durst Organization has signed :3Coffee Roasters to a 1,232-square-foot lease for a new retail location at 30 Halletts Point in Astoria, Queens. Expected to open later this year, the new shop marks an expansion for the family-owned business and its second Astoria location. It will also be the first retail at 20 and 30 Halletts Point, which opened last year with 647 apartments. “Halletts Point is a thriving community with spectacular views of Manhattan and Queens. As the neighborhood continues to grow, we are selecting retailers that will bring additional value to residents and neighbors alike, and we are excited to welcome :3Coffee Roasters,” said Jody Durst, president of The Durst Organization. :3Coffee Roasters was founded by Astoria residents Fabian Guzman and Andrea Gomez. The brand first opened on Steinway Street in Astoria and later expanded to the Flatiron District in Manhattan, building a following for their neighborhood-oriented approach and high-quality offerings. The Durst Organization was represented in-house by Karen Rose and Eric Engelhardt and by KSR’s Zach Nathan, Mark Gallucci, and Hunter Lazan. :3Coffee Roasters was represented by Genaro Otero at Sinvin. The post Astoria Favorite :3Coffee Roasters Expands to Halletts Point appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: :3Coffee Roasters signed 1,232 SF lease at 30 Halletts Point (Astoria, Queens); Durst Organization landlord.
Second Astoria location for family-owned brand; first retail at 20/30 Halletts Point (647 apartments opened 2025).
Building: walkable waterfront community with Manhattan views; neighborhood-oriented retail strategy emerging.
stories.summary: The Durst Organization signed :3Coffee Roasters, a family-owned specialty coffee brand, to a 1,232-square-foot retail lease at 30 Halletts Point in Astoria, Queens. This marks the brand's second Astoria location and represents the first retail opening at the newly completed 20 and 30 Halletts Point buildings, which together delivered 647 apartments in 2025. The expansion reflects the neighborhood's maturation and Durst's strategy to attract neighborhood-oriented retailers.
stories.impact: Halletts Point retail activation signals strong early-stage absorption and resident willingness to pay premium rents for walkable, mixed-use waterfront amenities in Queens. For multifamily developers: the retail success (local, independent tenancy) validates demand for authentic, neighborhood-serving commercial in emerging outer-borough submarkets. Signals strong rent-paying capacity for nearby ground-up development and may accelerate further supply in Astoria waterfront; monitor absorption curves and demographic composition (high-income households driving specialty retail demand).

stories.title: CBRE Arranges Debt on Advanced Manufacturing Campus in San Jose’s Golden Triangle
stories.excerpt: CBRE announced it arranged $67.4 million in financing for Forge North First, a mixed-phase industrial/R&D campus and advanced manufacturing development in San Jose’s Golden Triangle submarket. Mike Walker, Brad Zampa and Andy Gross of CBRE’s Debt & Structured Finance team in San Francisco arranged the five-year bridge loan with floating-rate, non-recourse financing from an institutional lender on behalf of Four Corners Properties and a West Coast-based institutional investor. “The combination of surging occupier demand and extremely limited supply positions Four Corners to create significant value at Forge North First,” said Zampa. Four Corners, an established local investor and developer founded in 2005, has invested in 50 buildings totaling 7.2 million square feet. In January 2026, Four Corners and its institutional partner acquired the existing 205,800-square-foot, five-building campus from BXP. The mixed-phase program includes comprehensive modernization of the existing campus and development of two advanced manufacturing buildings totaling approximately 239,000 square feet. Connect Industrial West is where industry leaders come together to share insights, build relationships, and identify what’s next for the sector. bullets: CBRE arranged $67.4M bridge loan for Forge North First; San Jose Golden Triangle advanced manufacturing/R&D campus.
Four Corners Properties + institutional investor own; acquired 205,800 SF campus from BXP in Jan 2026.

stories.summary: CBRE arranged a $67.4 million five-year floating-rate, non-recourse bridge loan for Forge North First, an industrial/R&D campus in San Jose's Golden Triangle submarket. Four Corners Properties and a West Coast institutional investor acquired the existing 205,800-square-foot, five-building campus from Boston Properties in January 2026 and plan comprehensive modernization plus 239,000 SF of new advanced manufacturing buildings. The lender highlighted surging occupier demand and extremely limited supply as value drivers.
stories.impact: Advanced manufacturing/R&D demand in Silicon Valley (post-BXP exit) signals institutional conviction in industrial real estate fundamentals and persistent supply scarcity in core West Coast tech corridors. For multifamily developers: tight industrial supply and high capex modernization costs on existing stock may raise land/development costs in San Jose Golden Triangle; however, concentrated employment growth (advanced manufacturing, tech R&D) drives strong rental demand in adjacent residential submarkets. Early signal of potential underwriting upside for multifamily in South Bay if household in-migration accelerates.

stories.title: Marcus & Millichap Closes Sale of Downtown Westfield Mixed-Use
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap arranged the sale of 251 North Ave. W., a mixed-use property in Westfield, NJ, for $5,260,000. Alan Cafiero, David Cafiero and Damien Rance of Marcus & Millichap exclusively marketed the property on behalf of the seller and procured the private buyer. “Downtown Westfield continues to be one of the most desirable mixed-use investment markets in New Jersey,” said Alan Cafiero, senior managing director investments in Marcus & Millichap’s New Jersey office. “The combination of a premier downtown location, immediate proximity to the train station and a strong, diverse tenant roster generated significant investor interest in this asset.” The property is a three-story, 17,831-square-foot building on a 0.18-acre lot with direct access to municipal commuter parking. It has nine suites and was renovated in 2014. The rent roll features a diverse mix of service-oriented tenants, including Columbia Bank, Edward Jones, the State of New Jersey, BAYADA Home Health Care and Rooster Spin. The post Marcus & Millichap Closes Sale of Downtown Westfield Mixed-Use appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Marcus & Millichap sold 251 North Ave. W., Westfield, NJ mixed-use property for $5.26M.
17,831 SF, three-story, nine suites; direct access to commuter rail; diverse tenants.
Westfield downtown described as 'most desirable mixed-use investment markets in NJ'—strong fundamentals.
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap closed the sale of 251 North Ave. W. in Downtown Westfield, New Jersey for $5.26 million. The 17,831-square-foot, three-story mixed-use property features nine suites with diverse tenants (Columbia Bank, Edward Jones, BAYADA Home Health Care, State of NJ, Rooster Spin) and direct access to commuter parking. The property benefits from proximity to the municipal train station.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development; Downtown Westfield sale reflects stable mixed-use fundamentals in NJ suburban submarkets with strong transit connectivity. Indirect signal: commuter-rail-adjacent suburban real estate remains attractive to institutional investors; multifamily developers should monitor Westfield and similar NJ Gateway corridor communities for rental-demand tailwinds from Philadelphia and NYC in-migration.

stories.title: Nuveen Green Capital Closes $281M Record C-PACE Loan for Boston Condos
stories.excerpt: The steady climb of commercial property assessed clean energy (C-PACE) financing around the U.S. has made its way to one of Boston’s tallest buildings. Millennium Partners has secured a $281 million C-PACE loan to implement energy efficiency upgrades at the 62-story Winthrop Center in Downtown Boston, the developer announced Friday afternoon. Nuveen Green Capital originated the fixed-rate loan under the Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) Massachusetts program which marked the largest C-PACE financing to date in the New England region, according to the lender. The condo inventory of the roughly 800,000 square-foot mixed-use building completed in 2023 attracted strong lender competition with many debt funds chasing the loan, according to a source familiar with the transaction. The C-PACE debt closed concurrently with a $575 million commercial mortgage backed securities (CMBS) loan led by Morgan Stanley for the office and retail portion of the tower according to a presale report from Moody’s. CoStar first reported the MP Trust 2026-WTRP single-asset-single-borrower deal for Boston’s largest building in the city’s financial district. The combined $856 million debt package takes out a prior construction loan from Cale Street in October 2020 after the London firm stepped in following another bank who backed out during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, according to sources. “We were honored to partner with MassDevelopment to recapitalize the largest C-PACE-financed project in New England, one that has helped reshape downtown Boston with state-of-the-art, energy-efficient residences,” Mike Doty, senior director of originations for NGC, said in a statement. Christopher Jeffries, founder of Millennium Partners, said in a statement that the C-PACE loan “recognizes the investments we have made in energy efficiency while providing long-term capital that supports the building’s enduring performance.” The PACE Massachusetts program was updated in June 2026
bullets: Nuveen Green Capital closed $281M C-PACE loan for Millennium Partners' Winthrop Center (Boston); record New England.
62-story, ~800K SF mixed-use building (completed 2023); condo inventory + office/retail potion.
Fixed-rate PACE financing; strong lender competition; concurrent $575M CMBS loan (Morgan Stanley) for office/retail.
stories.summary: Nuveen Green Capital originated a $281 million C-PACE loan for Millennium Partners' Winthrop Center, a 62-story, 800,000-square-foot mixed-use building completed in 2023 in Downtown Boston. The fixed-rate PACE financing is the largest C-PACE deal to date in New England. Strong lender competition reflects the condo inventory appeal. A concurrent $575 million CMBS loan led by Morgan Stanley financed the office and retail portions.
stories.impact: C-PACE financing growth for mixed-use buildings (especially condos) signals expanded debt-sourcing options for capital-intensive urban development; lower cost of capital for energy-efficiency retrofits improves NOI stability. For multifamily developers: condo-heavy mixed-use buildings attracting strong PACE/CMBS lender appetite in gateway markets; consider hybrid condos + rental segments as blended-return strategy in Boston, NYC, other dense urban markets. Monitor PACE program expansion and regulatory tailwinds in Northeast—may unlock refinancing optionality and cap-rate compression for completed assets.
